A national monument on the Pajarito Plateau near Los Alamos, New Mexico, protecting the homes of the Ancestral Puebloans who lived here from about 1150 to 1600. The plateau is made of tuff, soft volcanic ash from an eruption of the Valles Caldera 1.14 million years ago. The people cut its harder layers into blocks for building and dug rooms, called cavates, into the soft cliffs of Frijoles Canyon.

On the canyon floor stands Tyuonyi, a round pueblo once one to three storeys high, its roof beams dated by tree rings to between 1383 and 1466. Along the foot of the cliff runs Long House, built against the rock, and the rebuilt Talus House. Alcove House sits in a shelter cave 43 m above the canyon floor, reached by ladders, with a rebuilt kiva. The canyon was busiest in the 15th century, when groups moving from the drought-struck Four Corners region, home of Chaco and Mesa Verde, settled the Rio Grande valley. By 1600 the people had moved down to pueblos near the Rio Grande, such as Cochiti and San Ildefonso, which their Pueblo descendants still live in.

In 1880 José Montoya of Cochiti Pueblo brought the Swiss-American scholar Adolph Bandelier to the canyon, and his work led President Woodrow Wilson to create the monument on 11 February 1916. Crews of the Civilian Conservation Corps built its roads, trails and lodge from 1933 to 1941, in a style based on local pueblos. During the Second World War the lodge housed staff of the Manhattan Project at nearby Los Alamos.
